Unlike the DII, the EDIP is a data-driven food-based index that was developed using a combination of reduced-rank regression
and step-wise linear regression based on circulating concentrations of CRP, IL-6, and TNFa-R2. A total of 18 foods groups that
contribute either pro-inﬂammatory or anti-inﬂammatory properties in an overall dietary pattern were selected. A large prospective
study among 210,145 individuals with 9794 CHD cases found that individuals with higher scores on the EDIP, reﬂecting a more
pro-inﬂammatory diet, had a 46% higher risk of developing CHD. The EDIP was also associated with higher concentrations of pro-
inﬂammatory markers (IL-6, soluble intercellular adhesion molecule-1 [sICAM-1], TNFa-R1, TNFa-R2, CRP, and leptin) and lower
concentrations of an anti-inﬂammatory marker (adiponectin). Other studies have demonstrated positive associations between the
EDIP and cardiometabolic risk factors, including weight gain, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome.
The overall body of literature indicates that a higher inﬂammatory potential of diet is associated with a higher risk of CHD. The
DII and EDIP are two separate tools that can be used to characterize the inﬂammatory potential of diet. Further studies and reﬁne-
